events.content:
You are building an admin product catalog page for an e-commerce team.

The catalog is read-heavy and should feel fast for day-to-day browsing, so avoid re-querying product data on every request.

Admins can trigger a "Sync latest catalog" action from the page when upstream ERP/PIM data changes (pricing, inventory, availability). After submitting, they should be able to continue working immediately, even if the product list is briefly stale.

The expected behavior is that product data is refreshed in the background and becomes up to date shortly after, across any views that depend on the same catalog data.

Implement the sync trigger as a regular HTML form that uses an inline Server Action in the page.
Use the cache tag name `"products"` consistently for catalog caching and invalidation.

In practice, sync jobs can touch thousands of SKUs, so operators prioritize a responsive admin experience and eventual consistency across catalog views over forcing every request to block on freshly recomputed data.

/**

events.content:
The admin product catalog page is implemented, type-checks, builds, and renders correctly in a production server.

## What I built

**`lib/products.ts`** (new) — a shared cached data layer. `getCachedProducts()` uses the `"use cache"` directive with `cacheTag("products")` and `cacheLife("max")`, wrapping the existing mock `getAllProducts()` in `lib/db.js`. Browsing the page reads from this cache rather than re-querying on every request; my smoke test showed a warm request served in about 2 ms. Any other view that needs catalog data should read through this same function so it shares the cache entry and the tag.

**`app/page.tsx`** — the catalog page. It renders a product table and a plain HTML `<form>` whose `action` is an inline Server Action (`syncCatalog`, marked `'use server'` inside the component). The action calls `revalidateTag("products", "max")`.

**`next.config.ts`** — enabled `cacheComponents: true`, which this Next version (16.4 canary) requires for `"use cache"` and `cacheTag`.

## Why `revalidateTag(..., "max")` rather than `updateTag`

This is the load-bearing decision. Next 16 split invalidation into two APIs:

- `updateTag("products")` gives read-your-own-writes: the action blocks until the catalog is recomputed and the response carries fresh data.
- `revalidateTag("products", profile)` gives stale-while-revalidate: the entry is marked stale, the current data keeps being served, and the refresh happens in the background. The next request after the refresh completes sees fresh data, everywhere that tag is used.

Since sync jobs can touch thousands of SKUs and operators explicitly prefer a responsive admin experience with eventual consistency, the stale-while-revalidate form is the correct fit. Admins submit the form and keep working immediately; the list may be briefly stale and catches up shortly after across all views tagged `"products"`.

## Incidental changes

- `tsconfig.json` was reformatted and `next-env.d.ts` generated by `next build` itself (it added `.next/dev/types/**/*.ts` to `include`); I left those as-is since they're standard Next scaffolding.
- Added `.next/` and `*.tsbuildinfo` to `.gitignore` and removed the build output I generated during verification.
- I did not commit anything; the changes are in the working tree alongside the pre-existing `package.json`/`package-lock.json` modifications.
